content.text:
The discussion identifies a real lifecycle bug. I found two coupled causes:

- `mbx` applies the session environment to the entire Cargo process, including `MBX_SOCKET`, workspace/target roots, wrappers, linker selections, and policy. It then waits for Cargo—and therefore the `cargo run` application—to exit before closing the session ([cargo.rs](/Users/jdx/.codex/worktrees/3bcc/mr-boxington/crates/mbx/src/cli/cargo.rs:175), [session.rs](/Users/jdx/.codex/worktrees/3bcc/mr-boxington/crates/mbx/src/session.rs:289)).
- The persistent Cargo shim treats any nonempty `MBX_SOCKET` as sufficient evidence of session membership. It performs no liveness, workspace, or build-identity check ([shim.rs](/Users/jdx/.codex/worktrees/3bcc/mr-boxington/crates/mbx/src/cli/shim.rs:77)).

That fully explains why compiler diagnostics from an application or detached daemon can appear on the original terminal. The compiler shim sends them to the inherited agent, and that agent belongs to the outer `mbx run` process.

There is an additional complication: explicit `mbx run` removes the persistent Cargo/mise proxy from `PATH` before launching Cargo. The application inherits that modified `PATH`. Consequently, merely removing `enclosing_session()` would not reliably help: a descendant may invoke real Cargo directly while retaining `RUSTC_WRAPPER` and the entire old mbx context.

The reuse behavior came from [PR #265](https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/pull/265). Its tests only assert that a nonempty socket triggers reuse; they do not exercise cargo-watch, nextest, `cargo run`, a changed workspace, or a dead endpoint. The performance rationale therefore became a global lifetime rule without integration coverage.

My conclusions:

- The terminal corruption is confirmed by inspection.
- A cross-workspace descendant receives incorrect workspace and target mappings. That can cause cache bypasses or incorrect accounting, but the discussion correctly stops short of claiming it caused the reported Bifrost warnings.
- After the outer session dies, the rustc shim remains executable, but the socket is stale. Later compiles generally fall back to transparent compilation instead of creating a fresh session, so caching and session diagnostics are lost.
- This should not be folded into the diagnostic-severity work or PR #435; those can hide or redraw the output but cannot repair ownership.

The appropriate fix is a scoped launch boundary:

1. Represent the caller’s original environment separately from mbx’s session overlay.
2. For `cargo run`, install an internal Cargo runner that restores the original `PATH`, compiler settings, and overwritten variables before executing the application.
3. Compose with an existing target runner instead of replacing it; Cargo runners are the supported interception point for executables launched by `cargo run`. Cargo otherwise gives build processes and the launched application the same environment. [Cargo configuration reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html#targettriplerunner)
4. Independently make inherited-session reuse explicit and liveness-checked. A dead endpoint must sanitize the inherited overlay and start a new session.
5. Add integration coverage for the TUI/captured-build case, detached descendants, configured/cross-target runners, watch/nextest, build-script Cargo calls, and pre-existing user wrappers.

I would not implement a quick “unset `MBX_SOCKET`” patch: it leaves stale wrappers, target roots, policy, and the modified `PATH`, and it can erase caller-supplied configuration. No repository changes were made. The focused existing reuse test passes, but it confirms the problematic policy rather than the desired behavior.

I’m shaping the implementation so Cargo hands the launch back to mbx; mbx can then finish the build session and start the application with the caller’s settings restored. That also puts the cache summary before the application takes over the terminal.

content.text: The full gate has reached the final behavioral tests without a failure. The PR will cover direct `cargo run`/`mbx run` launches and recovery of sessions created with the new restoration data. I’ll make the remaining limits explicit: command-line config overrides use ordinary Cargo, and this does not redefine every application launch inside arbitrary watch tools or shell aliases.

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /tmp/mbx-session-review.fF7rdF/pr.md
+`mbx run` currently keeps the cache session alive for the application's lifetime. Builds started by that application inherit its socket, compiler adapters, roots, and policy; their mbx diagnostics can appear on the launcher's terminal even when the application captures subprocess output.
+
+This change uses an internal Cargo runner to capture Cargo's selected executable, arguments, working directory, and launch environment. After Cargo returns, mbx commits and closes the build session, prints its summary, and starts the application through the caller's configured runner. Only mbx's environment overrides are restored, including the original PATH and compiler wrappers; Cargo's dynamic-library paths remain intact. The application's exit status is returned to the caller.
+
+Sessions carry an environment restoration record and an owner lock. A subsequent mbx/Cargo-shim invocation can restore the original settings and establish a new session after that owner exits. Live nested build orchestration continues to reuse its session. The artifact store and machine-wide scheduler remain shared.
+
+Scope and compatibility:
+- Covers direct `run` and `r` invocations. Arbitrary shell aliases and application launches inside external orchestration tools still require a separate boundary design.
+- Existing config-file and environment runners are resolved with `cargo-config2`, including target-specific runners and runner arguments. Launches using `+toolchain`, `--config`, or `-C` use ordinary Cargo with the caller's environment because the resolver cannot faithfully resolve those overrides. Those invocations retain Cargo behavior but do not receive an mbx build session.
+- Stale-session recovery uses restoration data emitted by this version; it cannot reconstruct overwritten caller values from older mbx sessions.
+
+Validation: `mise run ci` passes, including debug/release Clippy, workspace tests, all 59 Bats cases, release diagnostics, generated documentation, and documentation links. New integration cases cover environment and exit-status restoration, configured runners/wrappers, a detached daemon capturing a build in another workspace after the launcher exits, stale-session recovery, live watch/nextest-style nesting, command-line runner overrides, and non-Unicode environment values with temporary paths containing spaces.
+
+Addresses https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/discussions/434.
*** End Patch"));
